claims.text: The starting catalyst is a multi-element automotive alloy with nearly equiatomic composition.
The starting catalyst has a disordered multi-principal-element structure.
Low-pressure nitrogen-plasma treatment at 150–250 °C for 10–30 minutes can form a surface nitride or oxynitride layer on the catalyst.
The plasma treatment can form the surface layer with minimal impact on the catalyst's bulk structure.
The resulting nitride or oxynitride film will be thin and coherent.
The resulting surface film will be enriched in transition metals from the alloy.
Surface nitride phases will act as a protective barrier against corrosive attack by H2O and NO.
The nitride or oxynitride surface film will inhibit catalyst sintering during thermal aging.
Plasma nitridation will modify surface electronic properties.
The modified surface electronic properties will optimize adsorption and reaction of exhaust intermediates.
The plasma-nitrided catalyst will have improved catalytic performance at low and transient temperatures relative to the untreated catalyst.
The plasma-nitrided catalyst will sustain its catalytic performance during low-temperature and transient operation.
The plasma-nitrided catalyst will resist deactivation and thermal aging better than the untreated catalyst.
The intervention will maintain minimal platinum-group-metal consumption relative to the untreated catalyst.
The untreated catalyst loses activity because of sintering.
The untreated catalyst is poisoned by H2O and NO.
The untreated catalyst degrades under thermal aging and long-mileage exposure.
Transient exhaust operation at 150–250 °C is typical of gasoline or hybrid vehicles.
